design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of adjusted odds ratios from prospective population cohorts that measured cannabis use before 18 and depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation or suicide attempts afterwards (inclusion asked for outcomes in young adulthood, 18 to 32), each adjusted at least for age, sex and baseline depression and/or anxiety. 35 longitudinal studies reviewed and 11 pooled (7 depression, 3 anxiety, 3 suicidal ideation, 3 suicide attempts; 23,317 individuals). Where a study reported several frequency categories, only the highest category against no use was pooled. Medline, Embase, CINAHL, PsycInfo and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses to 23 January 2017; risk of bias by the RTI item bank; no registered protocol. Meta-regression on depression measure and country; a propensity-score reanalysis of one cohort. Read in the corrected version (correction of 13 March 2019).
can_establish: The average adjusted association, in prospective cohorts published up to January 2017, between adolescent cannabis use (mostly the most frequent use category each study reported, against no use) and later depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation and suicide attempts, after adjustment for baseline depression or anxiety and the other covariates each study chose.
cannot_establish: That cannabis causes depression or suicidality (observational data; confounding and reverse direction are reduced only by baseline adjustment); absolute risks or a population attributable fraction (which needs causal assumptions and inputs the review does not supply); dose-response; a special window of risk in adolescence (adolescent and adult exposure were not compared); and, for suicidality, outcomes in young adulthood specifically, since two of three studies in each pool measured them in adolescence.

sample.recruitment: Database search designed by a health-sciences librarian, peer reviewed by a second librarian (PRESS), without language or date limits: Medline, Embase, CINAHL, PsycInfo and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses from inception to 23 January 2017, plus reference lists of included studies and reviews and a grey-literature search (Grey Matters) (Methods › Search Strategy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Participants came from population-based cohorts in the United States, Puerto Rico, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand (Figures 2 and 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: original articles in peer-reviewed journals; population-based data collected longitudinally and prospectively; exposure specifically cannabis; outcome depression, suicidal behaviour, anxiety or mixed anxiety-depression, controlled for at baseline; cannabis assessed before 18 (at least once) and the outcome assessed in young adulthood (18 to 32); results as odds ratios; adjusted for age, sex and baseline depression and/or anxiety. For cohorts reported several times, the report with the longest follow-up was chosen (Methods › Study Selection, 1st paragraph). Of 269 full texts, 234 were excluded, with reasons said to be in eTable 2 (not read); 24 of the 35 reviewed studies did not report poolable odds ratios or duplicated cohorts.
sample.demographics: Not given in the article; ages, sex distribution, sample sizes and definitions are in eTable 1 (not read). Countries by pooled study: United States (4, one with Puerto Rico), Canada (2), United Kingdom (1), Australia (1), New Zealand (2) and an Australian and New Zealand consortium (1) (Figures 2 and 3).
sample.attrition: Not reported for the included cohorts in the article.
sample.selection_effects: High-income countries only. Restriction to peer-reviewed articles (with an unexplained exception: a doctoral thesis is among the 35 reviewed studies), to studies reporting odds ratios and to adjusted estimates leaves 11 of 35 cohort studies in the pools; studies reporting regression coefficients, percentages or trajectories were summarized narratively. The search ended about two years before publication (online 13 February 2019).

exposure.measurement: As defined by each cohort, mostly self-report questionnaires; most measured frequency of use in the past year or past 6 months, distinguishing occasional, weekly and daily use; at least one pooled study used a cannabis use disorder diagnosis by 17 (Marmorstein and Iacono, 2011, as described in the reanalysis) (Methods › Parameters Definitions, 1st paragraph; Results › Sensitivity Analysis and Propensity Score Analysis, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: When a study reported several frequency categories, only the highest category against no use was pooled, so the contrast differs between studies (in one cohort it is a cannabis use disorder by 17); quantity and potency were not available, and the authors note that potency has risen since 1980 and varies by place (Methods › Parameters Definitions, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Handled only through each study's adjustment: the Methods say parental education, socioeconomic status, alcohol and cigarette smoking were controlled in almost all included studies, while the Limitations say not all studies adjusted for other drugs, cigarettes or psychosocial factors such as school dropout or peer drug use (Methods › Study Selection; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph). Per-study adjustment sets are only in eTable 1 (not read).

comparison.controls: Adolescents who did not use cannabis (non-use), within each cohort, by the review's pooling rule for studies that reported several frequency categories (highest category against no use); for the one pooled study whose exposure is a cannabis use disorder by 17 (Marmorstein and Iacono, 2011), the article does not state the comparison group.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level; every pooled odds ratio was adjusted at least for age, sex and baseline depression and/or anxiety (or, for suicidality, the outcome at baseline), with other covariates chosen by each study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors name school dropout and peer drug use as psychosocial factors not adjusted in all studies, and note that if depression is more frequent in people who use cannabis, adjusting for baseline depression would not remove it as a confounder (Results › Sensitivity Analysis and Propensity Score Analysis, 2nd paragraph). Family history of depression is mentioned only for the reanalysed cohort (parental major depression); childhood adversity and genetic liability are not mentioned in the article.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison groups did not use cannabis but could use alcohol, tobacco and other drugs; adjustment for these varied by study.

outcomes.instruments: Depression and anxiety as dichotomous outcomes from DSM-III or DSM-IV criteria or ICD-10, or from scales with cut-offs (for example SCL-90, CIDI, GHQ-12, CIS-R); suicidal ideation and attempts from questionnaires, interviews or scales (Methods › Parameters Definitions, 2nd paragraph). In the depression pool, four studies used DSM or ICD-10 criteria, one a structured interview, one a symptom checklist and one a dichotomous measure combining diagnostic interviews and the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Mix of diagnostic interviews and screening cut-offs; the authors call the methods of detecting major depression heterogeneous. Risk of bias was rated with the RTI item bank (29 items on precision and on selection, performance, attrition, detection, reporting and information bias), but no ratings are reported in the article (Methods › Quality Assessment).
outcomes.operationalization: Adjusted odds ratio for each outcome comparing the highest reported category of adolescent cannabis use with no use; timing of the outcome as reported by each study (in adolescence for two of three studies in each suicidality pool).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four pooled outcomes, two meta-regressions on the depression pool and one sensitivity analysis, without correction.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts; the abstract states that two reviewers conducted all review stages independently.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects pooled adjusted odds ratios (Figures 2 and 3, values printed with each study): depression 1.37 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.62), 7 studies, Q printed as 3.26 with 6 df (P = .62), I-squared 0%; anxiety 1.18 (0.84 to 1.67), 3 studies, Q 3.26 with 2 df (P = .20), I-squared 42%; suicidal ideation 1.50 (1.11 to 2.03), 3 studies, Q 1.49 (P = .48), I-squared 0%; suicide attempts 3.46 (1.53 to 7.84), 3 studies, Q 5.38 (P = .07), I-squared 61.3%. Depression by measure: structured diagnosis 1.38 (1.15 to 1.66) vs scales 1.28 (0.83 to 1.97), P = .74; by country: United States 1.54 (1.20 to 1.98) vs other countries 1.24 (0.99 to 1.56), P = .21. Without the overlapping Victorian cohort report: depression 1.40 (1.17 to 1.67). Editors' recalculation from the printed study estimates (DerSimonian-Laird on log odds ratios): depression 1.37 (1.16 to 1.62), Q 4.40, P = .62; anxiety 1.18 (0.85 to 1.65), Q 3.44, I-squared 42%; ideation 1.50 (1.10 to 2.04); attempts 3.48 (1.51 to 8.03), tau-squared 0.34 (fixed effect 2.70, 1.74 to 4.19); depression without the highest study (Marmorstein and Iacono, 2011) 1.33 (1.12 to 1.58). No prediction intervals or absolute risks are reported.
analysis.covariates: At review level, none; pooled odds ratios were adjusted within studies at least for age, sex and baseline depression and/or anxiety, and mostly for parental education, socioeconomic status, alcohol and smoking (per the Methods). Meta-regression covariates: depression measure (structured diagnosis vs scale) and country.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The meta-regression was planned with three country groups (Australia, United States, other countries) and reported as United States against other countries.
analysis.selective_reporting: Risk-of-bias ratings, per-study sample sizes, exposure definitions and adjustment sets are not in the article (supplement, not read). For studies with several frequency categories only the highest was pooled, by a stated rule. Only the depression pool was explored by meta-regression and sensitivity analysis.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Three of the four pools contain three studies each, so their random-effects intervals are unstable; the meta-regressions rest on seven studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 7 prospective cohorts, adolescents in the highest reported cannabis-use category had 1.37 times the odds (1.16 to 1.62) of later depression compared with those who did not use, after adjustment for baseline depression or anxiety and other covariates, with no detectable heterogeneity; only 2 of the 7 studies were individually significant. Anxiety: 1.18 (0.84 to 1.67) from 3 studies. Suicidal ideation: 1.50 (1.11 to 2.03) and suicide attempts: 3.46 (1.53 to 7.84; I-squared 61%), each from 3 studies, two of which in each pool measured the outcome in adolescence. The depression estimate barely changed without an overlapping cohort (1.40), and in the one reanalysed cohort propensity-score adjustment gave much the same estimate as regression (2.6 vs 2.5).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points advise that "Preadolescents and adolescents should avoid using cannabis" and call for preventive policy; the abstract says the high prevalence of use generates many young people who could develop depression and suicidality attributable to cannabis; the Discussion puts the population attributable risk at 7.2%, or 413,326 young adult cases of depression in the United States (corrected on 13 March 2019 from adolescent cases). Gaps: (1) attribution to cannabis assumes the association is causal, while the Limitations say a strong causal association cannot be made; (2) the attributable fraction is computed without a stated method; it can be reproduced (editors' calculation) by applying the pooled odds ratio as a relative risk to 20.9% past-month use among US adolescents, although the pooled contrast was the highest-use category against no use, and the case count multiplies the US population aged 18 to 34 by a 2-week prevalence of depression among adults over 20 that the same paragraph calls incidence; (3) the suicidality estimates are labelled young adulthood but two of three studies in each pool measured outcomes in adolescence, contrary to the inclusion criteria; (4) no association with anxiety (Key Points) rests on 3 studies with an interval up to 1.67, and the Results text says anxiety odds were increased; (5) the Key Points' statement that the association holds even without a premorbid condition overstates what adjustment for baseline depression achieves; (6) the propensity-score reanalysis of a single cohort, using the same measured covariates, cannot address unmeasured confounding, while a published propensity-score analysis with a null result (Harder et al., 2008) is mentioned but not pooled or explained; (7) the window of risk in adolescence, the imaging and animal paragraphs and the call for teaching skills to resist peer pressure go beyond the review's data. Against this, the depression pool is consistent across cohorts and adjusted for baseline depression, and the Limitations state the causal caveat and the heterogeneity of measures.

timeline.event: Paton, Kessler and Kandel (ref. 14), longitudinal analysis of depressive mood and adolescent drug use, cited to show the question has been studied since the 1970s.
Patton et al. (ref. 15), cohort study cited for a larger association in young women; among the 24 non-pooled studies.
Degenhardt, Hall and Lynskey (ref. 24), described here as a systematic review and meta-analysis of cannabis and depression in the general population, unable to isolate adolescent use.
Systematic review of psychotic and affective outcomes in the general population (ref. 23), cited as a predecessor that could not isolate adolescent use.

Harder, Stuart and Anthony (ref. 68): with propensity-score adjustment the association between adolescent cannabis problems and young adult depression became non-significant; mentioned as a reason for the review's own reanalysis, not pooled.

Marmorstein and Iacono (ref. 46), the cohort with the highest pooled odds ratio (2.62); its data were reanalysed for this review, which Marmorstein co-authored: 2.5 by logistic regression and 2.6 with propensity scores.
Degenhardt et al. (ref. 38), Victorian cohort, overlapping with the integrative analysis of three Australasian cohorts by Silins et al. (2014, ref. 10); removing it gave 1.40 (1.17 to 1.67).
Otten and Engels (ref. 69): depression risk after cannabis use higher in adolescents with the short serotonin-transporter allele (gene-environment interaction), cited narratively.

Lev-Ran et al. (ref. 22), meta-analysis of longitudinal studies of cannabis use and depression in youth and adults, which this review sets out to narrow to adolescent use; in the project's Tier B list.
Borges et al. (ref. 70), meta-analyses of cannabis use and suicidality, cited as earlier evidence on suicidal behaviour.

Wilkinson et al. (ref. 59): support for self-medication in males (more depressive symptoms at baseline, then more cannabis use) and no link from adolescent cannabis use to later depression, but one with tobacco; cited among the non-pooled null studies.
This review (online 13 February 2019), corrected 13 March 2019 (doi 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2019.0464): the attributable cases are young adult, not adolescent, cases.
Later cohort and co-twin tests in the project's lists, not appraised here: Hengartner et al. (2020, 30-year Zurich cohort) and Schaefer et al. (2022, co-twin control analyses of adult mental health).

replication.where_it_stands: A pooled adjusted association of modest size for depression (OR 1.37) that is consistent across seven cohorts, an imprecise null for anxiety, and suicidality estimates from three studies each, mostly with adolescent outcomes. The causal reading and the attributable-case figure are the authors'; the review's own Limitations, the propensity-score null of Harder et al. (2008) and the self-medication finding it cites keep residual confounding and reverse direction open. Claims should cite the depression odds ratio with its contrast (highest reported use category against no use, adjusted for baseline depression or anxiety and the covariates each cohort chose) and should not use the 7.2% or 413,326 figures; the suicide-attempt odds ratio should be quoted with its three studies and their adolescent outcomes. The overlap with Lev-Ran et al. (2014) and Silins et al. (2014) means these are not independent confirmations.

Two authors have funding or employment links with licensed cannabis producers. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: An individual-participant meta-analysis of the population cohorts with harmonized exposure (frequency, age at first use, product strength), outcomes measured in young adulthood by structured interview, the same adjustment set (including childhood adversity, family history of depression and other drug use), and designs that test unmeasured confounding and reverse direction (sibling or co-twin comparisons, repeated-measures models of which comes first), reporting absolute risks alongside odds ratios.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (adolescents under 18 in population cohorts), exposure (cannabis use), comparator (no use), outcomes (depression, anxiety, suicidality in young adulthood) and design stated (Methods › Study Selection).
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Prospective cohorts that control for baseline depression, explained by the high prevalence of depression among adolescents using cannabis at baseline (Introduction, 5th paragraph).

Strong search: five databases with a librarian-designed, peer-reviewed strategy, no language or date limits, reference lists and grey literature. But inclusion was restricted to original articles in peer-reviewed journals without a stated reason (criterion 1), which under item 4 as written (senior decision 21, which covers unexplained restrictions to peer-reviewed publications) is judged no; no registries or experts were consulted, and the search ended about two years before publication.
Two reviewers independently assessed all titles, abstracts and full texts (Methods › Study Selection).
The abstract states that two reviewers conducted all review stages independently; the Data Extraction section describes a structured DistillerSR form without naming the extractors.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the article states that eTable 2 lists all 269 full texts with the reason for each of the 234 exclusions; the supplement was not read, and Figure 1 gives only the total.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The article has no table of study characteristics; design, sample size, ages, exposure definitions, outcome measures and adjustment variables are said to be in eTable 1 (not read). The forest plots give only author, year and country.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The RTI item bank covers confounding balance, selection, performance, attrition, detection, reporting and information bias, a suitable technique; but no study-level or item-level ratings appear anywhere in the article, so how each study was judged cannot be checked (possibly in eTable 1, not read).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Adjusted odds ratios pooled with random-effects models, with Cochran Q and I-squared (Methods › Statistical Analysis). Weaknesses not scored by this item: the exposure contrast differs between studies (highest reported category), three pools have three studies each, outcomes measured in adolescence are pooled under young adulthood, and one Q value is misprinted (reporting issues). Judged met on balance.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of the impact of risk of bias on the pooled estimates; the sensitivity analysis addresses cohort overlap and the reanalysis one cohort's adjustment method.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Limitations say causal inference cannot be strong and that not all studies adjusted for other drugs, tobacco or psychosocial factors, but the risk-of-bias ratings are never reported or used, and the Discussion and Conclusions go on to count cases attributable to cannabis and to recommend that adolescents avoid it. A close call; judged not met because the interpretation does not carry the stated limitation.
Q and I-squared reported for each pool; heterogeneity in the depression pool explored by meta-regression on outcome measure and country (Results › Exploration of Heterogeneity via Meta-regression).
Not investigated: the Limitations argue publication bias is unlikely because cannabis was a primary predictor in the included studies, without a funnel plot, test or estimate of its likely impact.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and conflicts declared, including two authors' links with licensed cannabis producers (Article information).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 7 and 8 can be judged only from the supplement, which was not read; they cannot change the rating. Four critical items fail (2, no protocol; 4, unexplained restriction to peer-reviewed articles; 13, interpretation that does not account for risk of bias; 15, publication bias not investigated) and item 9 is only partly met, so confidence is critically low under AMSTAR 2. This rates the pooled odds ratios as summaries, not the review's usefulness: the search is strong, only adjusted estimates from prospective cohorts were pooled, and the depression estimate is stable (I-squared 0%; 1.40 without the overlapping cohort; editors' recalculation 1.33 without the highest study). In practice, the depression odds ratio of 1.37 is an adjusted observational association across differing exposure contrasts; the suicidality estimates rest on three studies each, mostly with adolescent outcomes; the anxiety null is imprecise; and the attributable-case figure is not a finding of the review: it applies the pooled odds ratio, taken as a relative risk, to the share of US adolescents with any past-month use, and assumes causation (key finding 12).

key_findings.finding: Search: health-sciences librarian strategy, peer reviewed by a second librarian (PRESS), no language or year limits; Medline, Embase, CINAHL, PsycInfo and ProQuest Dissertations and Theses from inception to 23 January 2017; reference lists of included studies and reviews; grey literature via Grey Matters; PRISMA followed; screening managed in DistillerSR.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search Strategy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Abstract › Data Sources

key_findings.finding: Flow: 5,071 records identified (Medline 1,788; PsycInfo 1,232; Embase 1,076; CINAHL 603; ProQuest 377); 1,929 duplicates removed; 3,142 screened; 2,877 excluded; 265 full texts plus 4 found through references (269); 234 excluded; 35 studies in the qualitative synthesis; 11 in the meta-analysis, comprising 23,317 individuals.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (printed counts, read from the rendered image); Abstract › Results
key_findings.note: The database counts sum to 5,076, not 5,071 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Inclusion: peer-reviewed original articles with population-based prospective data; cannabis as the exposure; depression, suicidal behaviour, anxiety or mixed anxiety-depression as outcomes, controlled for at baseline; cannabis assessed before 18 and the outcome in young adulthood (18 to 32); odds ratios adjusted at least for age, sex and baseline depression and/or anxiety; longest follow-up per cohort. Parental education, socioeconomic status, alcohol and smoking were also controlled in almost all included studies, by the authors' account in Study Selection, while Statistical Analysis says all studies reported odds ratios adjusted for prior depression and other confounders (for example sex, tobacco smoking, alcohol).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study Selection, 1st paragraph; Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exposure and outcome definitions: cannabis use mostly self-reported as frequency in the past year or past 6 months (occasional, weekly, daily); where several categories were reported, only the highest against no use was pooled. Depression and anxiety were dichotomous, by DSM-III or DSM-IV criteria or scale cut-offs (for example SCL-90, CIDI, GHQ-12, CIS-R); suicidal ideation and attempts by questionnaires, interviews or scales.

Depression in young adulthood, 7 studies: pooled adjusted OR 1.37 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.62), I-squared 0%. Study estimates: Brook et al. 2002 (US) 1.44 (1.08 to 1.91); Brook et al. 2011 (US and Puerto Rico) 1.50 (0.90 to 3.20); Degenhardt et al. 2013 (Australia) 1.10 (0.60 to 1.90); Gage et al. 2015 (UK) 1.30 (0.98 to 1.72); Georgiades and Boyle 2007 (Canada) 1.48 (0.65 to 3.40); Marmorstein and Iacono 2011 (US) 2.62 (1.22 to 5.65); Silins et al. 2014 (Australia and New Zealand) 1.02 (0.52 to 2.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Results of the Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 (estimates printed in the figure, read from the rendered image)
key_findings.note: Exposure: highest reported use category against no use (for the use-disorder study the article does not state the comparison group); adjusted for baseline depression or anxiety, age, sex and study-specific covariates (eTable 1, not read). Only Brook et al. 2002 and Marmorstein and Iacono 2011 exclude 1 on their own. The Q printed for this pool (3.26) does not match its P value (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Anxiety in young adulthood, 3 studies: pooled OR 1.18 (0.84 to 1.67), I-squared 42%: Brook et al. 2011, 1.60 (0.90 to 2.90); Degenhardt et al. 2013, 1.40 (0.84 to 2.50); Gage et al. 2015, 0.96 (0.75 to 1.24).
key_findings.locator: Results › Results of the Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
key_findings.note: Not statistically significant (abstract); the Results sentence nevertheless describes increased odds (see reporting issues). The interval is compatible with up to 67% higher odds.

key_findings.finding: Suicidal ideation, 3 studies: pooled OR 1.50 (1.11 to 2.03), I-squared 0%: Fergusson et al. 1996 (New Zealand) 1.40 (0.70 to 2.80); McGee et al. 2005 (New Zealand) 1.10 (0.58 to 2.07); Weeks and Colman 2016 (Canada) 1.74 (1.16 to 2.60). The Results state that two of these measured ideation within adolescence (Fergusson; Weeks and Colman) and one in young adulthood (McGee).
key_findings.locator: Results › Results of the Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph; Figure 3 (estimates printed in the figure)
key_findings.note: The only young-adult estimate in this pool is 1.10 (0.58 to 2.07).

key_findings.finding: Suicide attempts, 3 studies: pooled OR 3.46 (1.53 to 7.84), I-squared 61.3%: Roberts et al. 2010 (US) 4.81 (1.82 to 12.66); Silins et al. 2014 (Australia and New Zealand) 6.83 (2.04 to 22.90); Weeks and Colman 2016 (Canada) 1.87 (1.09 to 3.22). Attempts were measured within adolescence in two studies (Roberts; Weeks and Colman) and in young adulthood in one (Silins).
key_findings.locator: Results › Results of the Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: Editors' recalculation from the printed estimates: random effects 3.48 (1.51 to 8.03), tau-squared 0.34; fixed effect 2.70 (1.74 to 4.19). The most precise study gives 1.87.

key_findings.finding: Meta-regression on the depression pool: structured diagnostic tools 1.38 (1.15 to 1.66) vs scales 1.28 (0.83 to 1.97), P = .74; United States 1.54 (1.20 to 1.98) vs other countries 1.24 (0.99 to 1.56), P = .21.
key_findings.locator: Results › Exploration of Heterogeneity via Meta-regression, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analysis for overlapping cohorts: removing Degenhardt et al. (2013, Victorian Adolescent Health Cohort), part of which is also in Silins et al. (2014, with the Australian Temperament Project and the Christchurch Health and Development Study), gave a depression OR of 1.40 (1.17 to 1.67).
key_findings.locator: Results › Sensitivity Analysis and Propensity Score Analysis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' recalculation (DerSimonian-Laird from the printed study estimates): without Marmorstein and Iacono (2011), the highest study and a co-author's cohort, the depression OR is 1.33 (1.12 to 1.58).

key_findings.finding: Reanalysis of the Marmorstein and Iacono cohort (major depression by 24 predicted by cannabis use disorder by 17, adjusted for sex, parental major depression, major depression, alcohol use disorders and nicotine dependence by 17): OR 2.5 (1.1 to 5.5) by multivariable logistic regression and 2.6 (1.2 to 5.5) with propensity scores. The authors note that Harder et al. (2008) found the association non-significant with propensity-score methods, and that adjustment for baseline depression may not remove depression as a confounder.
key_findings.locator: Results › Sensitivity Analysis and Propensity Score Analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Propensity scores built from the same measured covariates do not address unmeasured confounding; Harder et al. (2008) is not among the pooled studies and the reason is not given.

key_findings.finding: Non-pooled evidence: 24 longitudinal studies reported regression coefficients, percentages or trajectories, or repeated cohorts. Most are described as finding a positive association with later depression; six found none, one of them supporting self-medication in males (more depressive symptoms at baseline, then more cannabis use) and linking tobacco rather than cannabis to later depression; one reported a gene-environment interaction (5-HTTLPR); in one trajectory study (1,232 college students) chronic and late-increasing use had the worst depression scores, and two trajectory studies found that stopping by the end of adolescence did not protect against some outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Systematic Review of Nonpoolable Studies and Trajectory-Based Studies, 1st to 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The narrative cites Degenhardt et al. (2013) as confirming higher depression risk with continued use to 29, whereas the estimate pooled from that study is 1.10 (0.60 to 1.90); the citation lists contain errors (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Population attributable risk: the Discussion gives 7.2% and translates it into 413,326 young adult cases of depression potentially attributable to cannabis, from a US population aged 18 to 34 of 70,872,118 and an incidence of depression of 8.1%, the same paragraph having given 8.1% as the share of US adults over 20 with depression in a 2-week period (2013-2016). A correction (13 March 2019) changed adolescent cases to young adult cases.
key_findings.note: No method is given. Editors' reconstruction: Levin's formula with 20.9% (past-month use among US adolescents, cited in the same paragraph) and OR 1.37 used as a relative risk gives 7.2%; 70,872,118 x 0.081 x 0.072 = 413,326. Not a finding of the pooled data; it assumes causation and mixes exposure definitions and a prevalence used as incidence.

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: no causal inference from the individual data, which were not reanalysed with causal methods; not all studies adjusted for other drugs, cigarettes or psychosocial factors (school dropout, peer drug use); heterogeneous depression measures; frequency rather than quantity; rising and variable potency. Publication bias was judged unlikely because cannabis was a primary predictor in the included studies; studies with cannabis as a secondary interest may have been missed.

Conclusions as stated: adolescent use is associated with increased risk of depression and suicidal behaviour later in life, even in the absence of a premorbid condition, and not with anxiety; adolescents should avoid cannabis; prevention programmes and teaching skills to resist peer pressure are urged, given a likely window of risk in adolescence.
key_findings.locator: Key Points › Findings and Meaning; Abstract › Conclusions and Relevance; Conclusions, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 2 prints the same heterogeneity statistic, Q = 3.26, for the depression pool (6 df, P = .62) and the anxiety pool (2 df, P = .20). With 6 df, Q = 3.26 would give P of about .78; recomputing from the printed study estimates gives Q of about 4.40 (P = .62) for depression and 3.44 (I-squared 42%) for anxiety (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The depression Q appears to be copied from the anxiety row; the conclusions (no detectable heterogeneity for depression) are unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say adolescent use was associated with increased odds of anxiety (OR 1.18, 0.84 to 1.67), while the abstract calls the pooled OR not statistically significant and the Key Points report no association.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Results of the Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Results; Key Points › Findings
reporting_issues.consequence: Both wordings misdescribe an imprecise estimate from 3 studies; a claim should give the interval.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criteria require outcomes in young adulthood (18 to 32), and the title and abstract describe suicidality in young adulthood, but the Results state that two of three studies in each suicidality pool measured the outcome within adolescence. The Introduction also gives exposure as 18 and younger, the Methods as younger than 18.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study Selection; Results › Results of the Meta-analyses, 1st paragraph; Introduction, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The suicidal ideation and suicide attempt estimates are mostly about adolescent outcomes; the only young-adult estimates are 1.10 (ideation) and 6.83 (attempts), one study each.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion's population attributable risk (7.2%; 413,326 cases) has no stated method, treats an odds ratio from the highest-use category as the effect of any past-month use, and calls a 2-week prevalence among adults over 20 the incidence of depression among people aged 18 to 34; the 13 March 2019 correction changed only adolescent to young adult cases.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; correction notice (doi 10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2019.0464)
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure applies the pooled odds ratio, taken as a relative risk, to an outside prevalence of any past-month use and assumes causation; it is not a finding of the pooled data and should not be quoted as one.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation errors in the lists of reviewed studies: reference 50, a 1993 meta-analytic review of children's peer relations, is cited among the 35 longitudinal studies and among those reporting a positive association between adolescent cannabis use and later depression; reference 34 (Brook et al., 2002), a pooled study, is cited among the non-pooled studies; and reference 49, a doctoral thesis, is among the 35 although the first inclusion criterion requires peer-reviewed articles. Minor: Weeks and Colman are dated 2016 in Figure 3 and 2017 in the reference list (ref. 57).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Data Extraction; Results › Systematic Review of Nonpoolable Studies and Trajectory-Based Studies, 1st paragraph; references 34, 49, 50
reporting_issues.consequence: The narrative count of positive and null non-pooled studies cannot be audited as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 gives 5,071 records, but the five database counts beneath it sum to 5,076; the exclusion box reads full-text articles excluded, through references.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the downstream counts (3,142; 269; 35; 11) are consistent with each other.

reporting_issues.issue: The Data Extraction section says the 35 longitudinal studies were retained for the meta-analysis, while only 11 were meta-analysed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor wording error; 35 is the systematic review, 11 the meta-analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The reanalysis supplement is titled for the cohort reported by Marmorstein and Iacono (2017), whereas the pooled study is dated 2011 (ref. 46); the reanalysis by logistic regression gives OR 2.5 (1.1 to 5.5) against 2.62 (1.22 to 5.65) plotted for the study, without comment.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Supplementary Materials list (eMethods 2); Results › Sensitivity Analysis and Propensity Score Analysis, 3rd paragraph; Figure 2
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; it is unclear whether the reanalysed data set is the same as the one pooled.

reporting_issues.issue: The meta-regression was planned with three country groups (Australia, United States, other countries) but reported as United States against all others.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Exploration of Heterogeneity via Meta-regression; Results › Exploration of Heterogeneity via Meta-regression, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A small deviation from the stated analysis; with 7 studies neither version has much power.

reporting_issues.issue: Methods › Statistical Analysis says all studies reported odds ratios adjusted for prior depression and other confounders (for example sex, tobacco smoking, alcohol); Methods › Study Selection says parental education, socioeconomic status, alcohol and smoking were controlled in almost all included studies, while the Limitations say not all studies adjusted for other drugs, cigarettes or psychosocial factors; the adjustment set of each pooled estimate is only in eTable 1.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph; Methods › Study Selection; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Which pooled estimates were adjusted for tobacco and other drugs cannot be checked from the article; claims should not state that the depression estimate is adjusted for them.
